sentences.t:
Ðā wæs hāten hreþe Heort innanweard
folmum gefrætwod;
sentences.l: Then was commanded quickly Heorot within with hands adorned;
sentences.i: Then it was ordered that Heorot be quickly adorned within by hands;
sentences.n: ‘wæs hāten’ is a past passive, ‘was commanded’, and with ‘gefrætwod’ (past participle, ‘adorned’) the sense is ‘Heorot was ordered to be adorned’; ‘folmum’ is a dative of means, ‘with hands’, and ‘innanweard’ is ‘within’. ‘hreþe’ is the crux: I take it as an adverb, ‘quickly’ (the usual form is ‘hraþe’), and that is a guess. The apparatus shows editors rewriting the phrase: Grundtvig and Bugge wanted ‘hēa(h)timbrede’ or ‘hēatimbred’ (‘high-timbered’) in place of ‘hāten hreþe’, and Trautmann ‘handum’ in place of ‘hāten’. ‘Heort’ is a short spelling of the hall’s name, ‘Heorot’, which Klaeber prints in full at 1017.

sentences.t:
fela þǣra wæs,
wera ond wīfa, þē þæt wīnreced,
gestsele gyredon.
sentences.l: Many of those there was, of men and of women, who the wine-hall, the guest-hall, made ready.
sentences.i: Many were the men and women who made the wine-hall, the guest-hall, ready.
sentences.n: ‘fela þǣra wæs’ is ‘many of those there was’: ‘fela’ is a noun that takes a genitive plural (‘þǣra’, ‘of those’) and here a singular verb, ‘wæs’. ‘wera ond wīfa’ (genitive plurals, ‘of men and of women’) says who they were. ‘þē’ is the relative particle, ‘who’, and its verb ‘gyredon’ (past plural of ‘gyrwan’, ‘to make ready, array’) has ‘wīnreced’ and ‘gestsele’ side by side as objects, two names for Heorot; the participle of the same verb is ‘gegyrede’ at 1028. ‘wīnreced’ is ‘wine-hall’ (‘reced’, ‘building’), as at 714, and ‘gestsele’ is ‘guest-hall’.

sentences.t:
Goldfāg scinon
web æfter wāgum, wundọrsīona fela
secga gehwylcum þāra þe on swylc starað.
sentences.l: Gold-variegated shone web along the walls, wonder-sights many to each of men of those who on such stare.
sentences.i: Tapestries shone gold-bright along the walls, a great many wonderful sights for every one of those who gaze on such things.
sentences.n: ‘scinon’ is the past plural of ‘scīnan’, ‘to shine’, with ‘web’ (‘woven work’, a neuter plural) as subject and ‘goldfāg’ agreeing with it; ‘fāg’ is ‘variegated, adorned’, so these are hangings worked with gold. ‘æfter wāgum’ is ‘along the walls’. ‘wundọrsīona fela’ is ‘many wonder-sights’: ‘fela’ takes the genitive plural of ‘sīen’, ‘sight’, and the phrase stands loosely beside ‘web’. ‘secga gehwylcum’ is ‘to each of men’, qualified by ‘þāra þe on swylc starað’, ‘of those who stare on such’ (‘starað’, plural of ‘starian’, with ‘on’ and the accusative). The dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘wundọrsīona’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre; it is the first one in this part, and ‘īrẹnbendum’ at 998 has another.

sentences.l: Was that bright building broken to pieces greatly, all inside, with iron bands fast, the hinges burst apart;
sentences.i: That bright building was badly shattered, all of it inside, though it was fastened with iron bands; its hinges were burst apart;
sentences.n: ‘Wæs … tōbrocen’ is a past passive, ‘was broken to pieces’, with ‘þæt beorhte bold’ (‘that bright building’) as subject and ‘swīðe’ (‘greatly’) and ‘eal inneweard’ (‘all inside’) as adverbs. ‘īrenbendum fæst’ is ‘fast with iron bands’, a dative of means: the hall was held together with iron and broke all the same. Holthausen shifts the line-end so that ‘īrenbendum’ starts the next line (apparatus), which would presumably take the bands with the hinges, ‘iron-bound hinges’; I keep Klaeber’s division. ‘heorras tōhlidene’ has no verb, so ‘were’ is understood: ‘heorras’ is ‘hinges’ and ‘tōhlidene’ the participle of ‘tōhlīdan’, ‘to burst apart, spring open’. The dot under the ‘ẹ’ in ‘īrẹnbendum’ is the same metrical sign as at 995.

sentences.t:
hrōf āna genæs
ealles ansund, þē se āglǣca
fyrendǣdum fāg on flēam gewand
aldres orwēna.
sentences.l: the roof alone survived all sound, when the awesome one, with crime-deeds stained, into flight turned, of life despairing.
sentences.i: only the roof came through entirely sound, once the fearsome one, stained with his crimes, had turned to flight, despairing of his life.
sentences.n: ‘hrōf āna genæs ealles ansund’ is ‘the roof alone came through, wholly unharmed’: ‘genæs’ is the past of ‘genesan’, ‘to survive’, ‘ealles’ a genitive used as an adverb, ‘ansund’ ‘sound’. ‘þē’ is the crux. As printed it is the relative particle, ‘who, which’, with nothing before it for it to refer to, and the clause needs ‘when’ or ‘after’; Thorpe, Holthausen, Sedgefield and others print ‘þā’ (apparatus), and I render ‘when’ as a guess. ‘āglǣca’ is the awesome one, Grendel. ‘fyrendǣdum fāg’ is ‘stained with crime-deeds’ (dative plural of means), ‘on flēam gewand’ is ‘turned to flight’ (past of ‘gewindan’), and ‘aldres orwēna’ is ‘hopeless of life’, with ‘aldres’ a genitive.

sentences.t:
Nō þæt ȳðe byð
tō befleônne — fremme sē þe wille —,
sentences.l: Not is that easy to flee from — let him do it who will —,
sentences.i: That is not easy to escape — let him try who will —,
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is the subject and points ahead to the fate described in the next lines. ‘ȳðe byð’ is ‘is easy’, the present of ‘bēon’ used for what holds at all times. ‘tō befleônne’ is an inflected infinitive, ‘to be fled from’, from ‘beflēon’ (the circumflex is the house mark for a contracted vowel). ‘fremme sē þe wille’ is a present subjunctive of ‘fremman’, ‘to do, carry out’, in a command: ‘let him do it who will’, a challenge to anyone who thinks he can. The dashes set the challenge aside from the sentence.

sentences.t:
ac gesēcan sceal sāwlberendra
nȳde genȳdde, niþða bearna,
grundbūendra gearwe stōwe,
þǣr his līchoma legerbedde fæst
swefeþ æfter symle.
sentences.l: but must seek — of soul-bearers, by need compelled, of the sons of men, of earth-dwellers — the ready place, where his body, fast in its lying-bed, sleeps after the feast.
sentences.i: But every one of the living, the sons of men and dwellers on the earth, driven by need, must seek out the place made ready, where his body lies fast in its bed and sleeps after the feast.
sentences.n: ‘gesēcan sceal’ is ‘must seek out’, and the subject is left unstated: ‘sāwlberendra’, ‘niþða bearna’ and ‘grundbūendra’ are genitive plurals (‘of soul-bearers’, ‘of the sons of men’, ‘of earth-dwellers’) that name the class, and the nominative participle ‘genȳdde’ (‘compelled’) shows the subject is one person of that class. ‘nȳde genȳdde’ is ‘compelled by compulsion’, ‘nȳde’ a dative of means. Klaeber’s italic ‘ē’ marks his change of the manuscript’s ‘ge sacan’ to ‘gesēcan’; Kemble and later editors print the same, while Schücking keeps ‘gesacan’. ‘gearwe stōwe’ is the accusative, ‘the ready place’, the grave. ‘legerbedde fæst’ is ‘fast in its lying-bed’, and ‘swefeþ æfter symle’ is ‘sleeps after the feast’; I read the feast as the feast of life, a guess.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs sǣl ond mǣl,
þæt tō healle gang Healfdenes sunu;
sentences.l: Then was season and time, that to the hall went Healfdene’s son;
sentences.i: Then the season and the hour had come for Healfdene’s son to go to the hall;
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs sǣl ond mǣl’ is ‘then was season and time’: ‘sǣl’ is a favourable occasion and ‘mǣl’ an appointed time, two near-synonyms joined as the subject of ‘wæs’, a phrase for ‘the right moment had come’. ‘þæt’ opens a clause that says what the moment was for: ‘that Healfdene’s son went to the hall’. ‘gang’ is a past form of ‘gangan’ (the commoner past is ‘gēong’, as at 925). ‘Healfdenes sunu’ is Hrothgar, named by his father, as elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t: wolde self cyning symbel þicgan.
sentences.l: would himself the king the feast partake.
sentences.i: The king himself wished to share in the feast.
sentences.n: ‘wolde’ is the past of ‘willan’, ‘wished’, with ‘þicgan’ (‘to take, receive, partake of’) as its infinitive. ‘self cyning’ is ‘the king himself’, ‘self’ an adjective in the nominative beside ‘cyning’. ‘symbel’ is the accusative object, ‘feast’, the formal banquet, as at 618.

sentences.t:
Ne gefrægen ic þā mǣgþe māran weorode
ymb hyra sincgyfan sēl gebǣran.
sentences.l: Not have I heard that kindred with a greater troop around their treasure-giver better bear themselves.
sentences.i: I have never heard of a people bearing themselves better, with a larger company, around their giver of treasure.
sentences.n: ‘Ne gefrægen ic’ is ‘I have not heard’, a fixed phrase (‘gefrægn ic’ at 1027) that takes an accusative and an infinitive: ‘þā mǣgþe … sēl gebǣran’, ‘that people bore themselves better’. ‘mǣgþe’ is the accusative of ‘mǣgþ’, here ‘tribe, kindred’ (at 943 the related form ‘mægþa’ was ‘of maidens’, ‘women’, with the note there). ‘māran weorode’ is a dative of accompaniment, ‘with a greater troop’, and ‘sēl’ is the adverb ‘better’. ‘gebǣran’ is ‘to bear oneself, behave’. ‘sincgyfan’ is the accusative of ‘sincgyfa’, ‘treasure-giver’ (‘sinc’, ‘treasure’, and ‘gifa’, ‘giver’), a kenning for the king: the word names the king by what a lord was expected to do, give out treasure.

sentences.l: Bowed then to the bench the glory-possessing ones, rejoiced in the fill, fairly received many a mead-cup;
sentences.i: Then the glorious company sat down on the bench, rejoiced in their fill, and took many a cup of mead with good grace;
sentences.n: ‘Bugon’ is the past plural of ‘būgan’, ‘to bow, bend, turn’, here ‘went to and took their seats’, as in ‘bowed then to the bench’ at 327. The subject ‘blǣdāgande’ is a present participle in the plural, ‘glory-possessing’ (‘blǣd’, ‘success, glory’, and ‘āgan’, ‘to own’). ‘fylle gefǣgon’ is ‘rejoiced in the fill’: ‘gefǣgon’ is the past plural of ‘gefēon’ and takes a genitive or dative, ‘fylle’, the fill of food and drink. ‘fægere’ is ‘fairly, courteously, with good grace’, ‘geþǣgon’ the past plural of ‘geþicgan’, ‘to receive’, and ‘medoful manig’ is ‘many a mead-cup’, ‘ful’ being a drinking cup.

sentences.t:
māgas wǣra[n]
swīðhicgende on sele þām hēan,
Hrōðgār ond Hrōþulf.
sentences.l: the kinsmen were strong-minded in the hall, the high one, Hrothgar and Hrothulf.
sentences.i: the kinsmen, Hrothgar and Hrothulf, were stout of heart in the lofty hall.
sentences.n: ‘wǣra[n]’ is Klaeber’s repair: the manuscript has ‘þara’, his italic ‘wǣ’ replaces ‘þa’ and the bracketed ‘n’ is added, giving ‘wǣran’, ‘were’, the verb the sentence needs (ten Brink and Holthausen print ‘wǣron’, Schücking and Sedgefield ‘wāron’). ‘māgas’ is a nominative plural, ‘kinsmen’, and ‘Hrōðgār ond Hrōþulf’ stands in apposition to it. ‘swīðhicgende’ is a present participle, ‘strong-minded’, and ‘on sele þām hēan’ is ‘in the hall, the high one’, the formula used in Fitt XI. Hrothulf is not explained here: the passage calls the two simply ‘māgas’, ‘kinsmen’, and I add nothing to that.

sentences.t:
Heorot innan wæs
frēondum āfylled;
sentences.l: Heorot within was with friends filled;
sentences.i: Heorot inside was filled with friends;
sentences.n: ‘Heorot innan wæs … āfylled’ is a past passive, ‘Heorot within was filled’, with the name placed before ‘innan’, and ‘frēondum’ is a dative of means, ‘with friends’. ‘Heorot’ (‘hart, stag’) is the name of the hall. The friends are presumably the Danes and the Geats seated together after the fight; the line does not say.

sentences.t:
nalles fācenstafas
Þēod-Scyldingas þenden fremedon. —
sentences.l: not at all treachery-deeds the People-Scyldings then performed. —
sentences.i: The Scyldings, the whole people, were doing no acts of treachery then. —
sentences.n: ‘nalles’ is ‘not at all’, and with ‘fremedon’ (past plural of ‘fremman’, ‘to do, perform’) it makes the whole clause negative: ‘fācenstafas’, the accusative plural object, were not done. ‘fācen’ is ‘deceit, treachery’ and ‘stæf’ ‘staff, letter’; I take the compound as ‘treacherous deeds’, and how the second half gives that sense is a guess. ‘Þēod-Scyldingas’ is ‘people-Scyldings’, the Danish nation as a whole (‘þēod’, ‘people’). ‘þenden’ is usually ‘while, as long as’; I take it as ‘then, at that time’ (or ‘while this lasted’), which limits the claim to the time of the feast, and the line says nothing about later. The dash marks a break before the gifts.

sentences.l: Gave then to Beowulf the child of Healfdene a banner golden, as victory’s reward, an adorned hilt-standard, helm and mail-shirt;
sentences.i: Then the son of Healfdene gave Beowulf, as a reward for his victory, a golden banner, an adorned standard, a helmet and a mail-shirt;
sentences.n: ‘Forgeaf’ (‘gave’) takes the dative ‘Bēowulfe’ for the receiver and accusative objects: ‘segen gyldenne’ (‘a golden banner’, ‘segen’ from Latin ‘signum’), ‘hiltcumbor’ with ‘hroden’ (‘adorned’, a past participle), ‘helm’ and ‘byrnan’. Whether ‘hroden hiltcumbor’ is a second item or restates the banner is not settled; I list it as a separate item. ‘sigores tō lēane’ is ‘as reward of victory’. The subject ‘bearn Healfdenes’ is Hrothgar; Klaeber’s italic ‘earn’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘brand’ (‘fire, sword’), and Grundtvig’s ‘bearn’ (‘child’) gives the sentence the giver it needs. Italic ‘t’ marks ‘hiltcumbor’: the manuscript has the two words ‘hilte cumbor’, several editors read ‘hilde-’ (‘battle-standard’), and Klaeber follows Cosijn’s ‘hilt-’. I take ‘cumbor’ as a banner or standard, and ‘hilt-standard’ is a guess at an uncertain compound; the idiomatic line leaves out the doubtful ‘hilt-’.

sentences.t:
mǣre māðþumsweord manige gesāwon
beforan beorn beran.
sentences.l: a famous treasure-sword many saw before the warrior borne.
sentences.i: Many saw a famous treasure-sword carried before the warrior.
sentences.n: ‘gesāwon’ (‘saw’, past plural, with ‘manige’, ‘many’, as subject) takes an accusative and an infinitive: ‘mǣre māðþumsweord … beran’, ‘a famous treasure-sword to be borne’, so the sword is what is carried. ‘beforan beorn’ is ‘before the warrior’ (preposition with the accusative), ‘beorn’ being Beowulf. ‘māðþumsweord’ is ‘treasure-sword’ (‘māðþum’, ‘treasure’), a sword that is itself a treasure. The sword is borne in front of him where many can see it.

sentences.t:
Bēowulf geþah
ful on flette;
sentences.l: Beowulf received a cup in the hall;
sentences.i: Beowulf accepted a cup in the hall;
sentences.n: ‘geþah’ is the past of ‘geþicgan’, ‘to receive, accept’, the verb whose plural is ‘geþǣgon’ at 1014; Holthausen prints ‘geþeah’ (apparatus). ‘ful’ is the accusative object, ‘a cup’, and ‘on flette’ is a dative, ‘in the hall’ (‘flet’ is the floor of the hall, where the feast was held). The cup is presumably the one offered to the guest of honour; the line does not say.

sentences.t:
nō hē þǣre feohgyfte
for sc[ē]oten[d]um scamigan ðorfte, —
sentences.l: not he of that fee-gift before the shooters to be ashamed needed, —
sentences.i: He had no cause to be ashamed of that gift before the warriors, —
sentences.n: ‘nō … ðorfte’ is ‘did not need’, the past of ‘þurfan’ with the infinitive ‘scamigan’, ‘to be ashamed’, which takes a genitive of the cause: ‘þǣre feohgyfte’, ‘of that fee-gift’ (‘feoh’, ‘wealth’, and ‘gifu’, ‘gift’). ‘for scēotendum’ is ‘before the shooters’, the warriors present. The manuscript has ‘scotenum’, which gives no clear word here; Kemble’s second edition and four later editors read ‘scēotendum’ (the present participle of ‘scēotan’, ‘to shoot’, in the dative plural), and Klaeber’s brackets mark the ‘ē’ and ‘d’ he adds.

sentences.t:
ne gefrægn ic frēondlīcor fēower mādmas
golde gegyrede gummanna fela
in ealobence ōðrum gesellan.
sentences.l: not have I heard friendlier four treasures, with gold adorned, many of men on the ale-bench to another give.
sentences.i: I have never heard of many men giving another, on the ale-bench, four treasures adorned with gold in a friendlier way.
sentences.n: ‘ne gefrægn ic’ is the poet’s ‘I have not heard’ again (see 1011), with an accusative and infinitive: ‘gummanna fela … gesellan’, ‘many of men to give’, where ‘fela’ with a genitive plural is the subject. ‘frēondlīcor’ is a comparative adverb, ‘in a friendlier way’, ‘fēower mādmas’ the object and ‘golde gegyrede’ a past participle, ‘arrayed with gold’ (the verb of ‘gyredon’ at 994). ‘ōðrum’ is ‘to another’. ‘ealobence’ is ‘ale-bench’, the drinking place in the hall. The poet says four. The things named at 1020–1023 are the banner, the ‘hiltcumbor’, the helmet, the mail-shirt and the sword: five if the banner and the ‘hiltcumbor’ are separate, four if ‘hroden hiltcumbor’ restates the banner, and the sword is said only to be carried before Beowulf, not to be given. Which four the poet counts is open.

sentences.t:
Ymb þæs helmes hrōf hēafodbeorge
wīrum bewunden wala ūtan hēold,
þæt him fēla lāf frēcne ne meahte
scūrheard sceþðan, þonne scyldfreca
ongēan gramum gangan scolde.
sentences.l: About the helmet’s roof, as head-protection, with wires wound, a ridge outside held, so that him the files’ leaving fiercely could not, shower-hard, harm, when the shield-warrior against the fierce ones to go should.
sentences.i: Around the crown of the helmet a ridge wound with wires guarded the head on the outside, so that no blade left by the files, hard-tempered as if in showers, could fiercely harm him when the shield-warrior had to go against his enemies.
sentences.n: ‘wala … hēold’ is ‘a ridge held’ (‘wala’, ‘ridge’, is a rare word and the sense is a guess from the context), with ‘wīrum bewunden’ (‘wound with wires’) agreeing with ‘wala’, ‘ymb þæs helmes hrōf’ (‘around the helmet’s roof’, the crown), ‘hēafodbeorge’ (‘head-protection’, saying what the ridge was for) and ‘ūtan’ (‘from outside’). The manuscript has ‘walan’; Klaeber’s italic ‘a’ marks his change, Sievers, Bugge and Sedgefield print ‘walu’. The result clause ‘þæt him … ne meahte … sceþðan’ is ‘so that it could not harm him’. The subject ‘fēla lāf’ is ‘the leaving of files’ (‘fēla’ a genitive plural), a sword the file has finished (the manuscript has ‘laf’ and ‘meahton’, plural; Klaeber’s italic ‘e’ in ‘meahte’ makes the verb singular to match; Grein and others read ‘lāfe’). ‘scūrheard’ (‘shower-hard’) may mean tempered in water or hard in the showers of battle, a guess. ‘scyldfreca’ is the wearer, Beowulf by implication; ‘gramum’ is ‘the fierce ones’.

sentences.l: Bade then the shelter of earls eight horses with plated cheeks into the hall to lead, in under the enclosures;
sentences.i: Then the protector of earls ordered eight horses with ornamented cheek-pieces to be led into the hall, in under the enclosing walls;
sentences.n: ‘Heht’ is the past of ‘hātan’, ‘to bid’, and takes an accusative and an infinitive: ‘eahta mēaras … teôn’, ‘eight horses to lead’; ‘mēaras’ is the plural of ‘mearh’, a poetic word for horse. ‘eorla hlēo’ (‘shelter of earls’) is most likely Hrothgar, the giver since 1020, but the line does not name him, and the same phrase meant Beowulf at 791. ‘fǣtedhlēore’ is ‘with plated cheeks’: ‘fǣted’ (‘plated, ornamented’) and ‘hlēor’ (‘cheek’), which I read as the cheek-pieces of the bridles, a guess. ‘on flet’ is ‘into the hall’. ‘in under eoderas’ is a crux: ‘eoderas’ is the accusative plural of ‘eodor’, ‘fence, enclosure’, so the horses are led in beneath some enclosing structure, but whether it is the hall’s walls, a court or a screen is unknown, and ‘the enclosing walls’ is a guess. ‘eodor’ also means ‘protector, lord’ at 1044, as at 426; the lexica may list that as a separate word or as the same word used figuratively.

sentences.t:
þāra ānum stōd
sadol searwum fāh, since gewurþad;
sentences.l: of those, on one stood a saddle with skilful work variegated, with treasure honoured;
sentences.i: On one of them stood a saddle adorned with skilled work and enriched with treasure;
sentences.n: ‘þāra ānum’ is a dative, ‘on one of them’, and ‘stōd’ takes ‘sadol’ as its subject; a bare dative of place is odd, so Holthausen puts ‘[on]’ before ‘ānum’ (apparatus), and I take the sense as ‘on one of them’ either way. ‘searwum fāh’ is ‘variegated with skilful work’ (‘searu’, ‘art, device’, a dative plural of means), ‘since gewurþad’ is ‘honoured, adorned with treasure’, the participle of ‘gewurþian’.

sentences.t:
þæt wæs hildesetl hēahcyninges,
ðonne sweorda gelāc sunu Healfdenes
efnan wolde, —
sentences.l: that was the battle-seat of the high king, when the sword-play Healfdene’s son to perform would, —
sentences.i: That was the war-saddle of the high king, when the son of Healfdene wished to take part in the play of swords —
sentences.n: ‘þæt wæs hildesetl’ is ‘that was the battle-seat’: ‘sadol’ is the saddle, ‘hildesetl’ (‘hilde’, ‘battle’, and ‘setl’, ‘seat’) restates it, and ‘hēahcyninges’ (‘of the high king’) is Hrothgar’s own. ‘ðonne … efnan wolde’ is ‘when … wished to perform’, ‘efnan’ meaning ‘to carry out, do’, with ‘sweorda gelāc’ (‘sword-play’, that is, battle) as object and ‘sunu Healfdenes’ as subject. The saddle stands on one of the horses that Beowulf is given at 1043, so Hrothgar’s own war-saddle presumably passes to him with it. The dash opens a comment on how he fought.

sentences.t:
nǣfre on ōre læg
wīdcūþes wīg, ðonne walu fēollon.
sentences.l: never at the front lay the far-known one’s war, when the slain fell.
sentences.i: the far-famed king’s fighting never flagged at the front, when men fell slain.
sentences.n: This clause is a crux. ‘nǣfre on ōre læg’ is literally ‘never lay at the front’: ‘ōr’ is ‘beginning, point, front’ and ‘læg’ the past of ‘licgan’, ‘to lie’. ‘wīdcūþes wīg’ is ‘the far-known one’s fighting’, ‘wīdcūþes’ being a genitive and ‘wīg’ the subject, so his fighting never lay down in the van. I read ‘lay’ as ‘failed, gave out’, a guess; other readings of ‘on ōre’ are possible. ‘ðonne walu fēollon’ is ‘when the slain fell’: I take ‘walu’ as the plural of ‘wæl’, ‘the slain’.

sentences.l: And then to Beowulf of each of the two the fence of the Ingwine possession granted, of horses and of weapons;
sentences.i: And then the guardian of the Danes granted Beowulf possession of both, horses and weapons;
sentences.n: ‘getēah’ is the past of ‘getēon’, ‘to grant’, with ‘Bēowulfe’ as the dative receiver, ‘onweald’ (‘power, possession’) as the accusative object and ‘bēga gehwæþres’ (‘of each of the two’) as a genitive depending on ‘onweald’, ‘power over each of the two’; ‘wicga ond wǣpna’ (‘of horses and of weapons’) names the two. ‘eodor Ingwina’ is ‘protector of the Ingwine’, ‘eodor’ here being the ‘fence’ of 426 used of a king, ‘protector, lord’; ‘Ingwine’ are literally ‘friends of Ing’, and who Ing was is not settled here (an ancestral figure of the Danes is the usual guess). The gift is a grant of ownership.

sentences.t: hēt hine wēl brūcan.
sentences.l: bade him well enjoy.
sentences.i: and told him to use them well.
sentences.n: ‘hēt’ is the past of ‘hātan’, ‘to bid’ (‘heht’ at 1035 is another form of the same past). It takes ‘hine’ as accusative of the person and ‘brūcan’ (‘to use, enjoy’) as infinitive; ‘brūcan’ governs a genitive or instrumental, here understood from the horses and weapons just named. ‘wēl’ is ‘well’.

sentences.t:
Swā manlīce mǣre þēoden,
hordweard hæleþa heaþorǣsas geald
mēarum ond mādmum, swā hȳ nǣfre man lŷhð,
sē þe secgan wile sōð æfter rihte.
sentences.l: So manly the famed lord, hoard-guard of heroes, battle-rushes repaid with horses and treasures, so that them never a man blames, he who to say will truth according to right.
sentences.i: So nobly did the famed lord, the heroes’ hoard-keeper, repay the onrushes of battle with horses and treasures, that no man who is willing to speak the truth rightly will ever find fault with them.
sentences.n: ‘Swā manlīce’ (‘so manly’, adverb) answers ‘swā hȳ nǣfre man lŷhð’, ‘so that no man ever blames them’. The subject is ‘mǣre þēoden’ with ‘hordweard hæleþa’ (‘hoard-guard of heroes’) in apposition; ‘geald’ is the past of ‘gieldan’, ‘to pay back’; ‘heaþorǣsas’ is the accusative plural, ‘battle-rushes’ (as at 557), the charges of battle that Beowulf made, and ‘mēarum ond mādmum’ is a dative of means. ‘lŷhð’ is a crux: I take it as the present of ‘lēan’, ‘to blame’, with ‘hȳ’ (‘them’) as object, a guess; the line does not say who ‘them’ is, and the gifts are the nearest plural. Sievers proposes ‘[ne] lyhð’ or ‘lēið’ (apparatus), so the form is unsettled. ‘sē þe secgan wile sōð æfter rihte’ is ‘he who will say the truth according to right’.
